about: Shipped with Looking Glass (attack_map.py). The SUGGESTED MITRE ATT&CK techniques for each Shadowserver report, from its name, type and group. The first rule that matches a report gives its suggestion, which a researcher confirms or changes on the Definitions page; a reviewed mapping is never replaced by a suggestion. certainty: observed = the report saw it happen; possible = an exposure an attacker could use. role: used = 'this device was used for ...'; target = 'this address was the target of ...'; host = 'this host was used for ...'; exposure = 'attackers can use this exposure for ...'. shortlist: the techniques the picker offers first. Reports no rule matches are 'not mapped yet' and are asked about on the Definitions page.

rules.why: The device looked up a command-and-control name that now points at a sinkhole (C2 over DNS).
The device contacted a sinkholed command-and-control server over HTTP (C2 over web protocols).
The device contacted a sinkholed command-and-control server (C2 over web protocols or DNS).
The device contacted infrastructure of malware used to sell access to victims (command and control).
The device tried to log in to a decoy system by guessing passwords.
Decoy amplifiers received forged requests in this address's name: it was the target of a reflection attack.
The device took part in a denial-of-service attack.
The network lets devices send packets with forged sender addresses, which reflection attacks depend on.
The device scanned the internet (it reached decoy systems looking for services).
The device sent traffic to unused address space, as scanning does.
The host served malware or a link to it (drive-by delivery, traffic distribution).
Malware run in a sandbox connected to this host: it serves the malware's command and control.
Malware run in a sandbox looked up names that resolve to this host.
A link to this host was found in spam (phishing by link).
The organisation was named as a ransomware victim (data encrypted or stolen for extortion).
An open proxy or tunnel: attackers can send their traffic through it and hide behind its address.

group: Can be abused for attacks (amplification, tunnels)

rules.why: The service answers small forged requests with large replies: attackers can use the host as a tool to flood someone else (the victim is elsewhere).
The service answers small forged requests with large replies: attackers can use the host as a tool to flood someone else (the victim is elsewhere).
A remote access or management service open to the internet: attackers can log in or take control through it.
An industrial control system reachable from the internet: attackers can connect to it directly.
A database or data service open to the internet: attackers can read or change the data it holds.
A public-facing service with a known weakness: attackers can exploit it to get in.
